title: Who Checks the AI's Work?
author: Magnetiz.ai
excerpt: Something in your GTM motion already drafts, scores or sends work you never watched get made. Asking the AI to check its own work has a known bias. Here is the review setup that holds up, and the three questions to ask any vendor.
content:
How to review AI output before it reaches your prospects, when you didn’t watch it get built.

If you run AI anywhere in your GTM motion, something already drafts, scores or sends work you never watched get made.

The outreach agent wrote 200 messages overnight. The scoring model ranked this week’s accounts. The research agent filled in the CRM.

The usual safeguard is asking the AI to check its own work. It says everything looks good, and it is usually right. The times it is wrong are the messages that reach a prospect.

A better setup takes a standard written before the work, a reviewer that starts cold, and a short list of rules nothing is allowed to break. Here is how to build it.

Why doesn’t "the AI checked its own work" count?

Same context, same assumptions.

When the agent that drafted the messages also reviews them, it starts with every assumption behind the draft already in view. If it decided a prospect’s old title was current, it checks against that same belief and finds nothing wrong.

The research points the same way. A NeurIPS 2024 study found that AI models used as judges can recognize their own output and score it higher than human raters would.

// WATCH FOR
Watch for a review step that has never once sent work back.

How do you write the standard before the work starts?

Criteria first. Output second.

For every workflow, write down what a passing output looks like when the task is created. For an outreach agent that might be under 65 words, one real buying signal named, no links, and no account that is already a customer.

Written first, the criteria cannot bend to fit whatever the agent produced.

// WATCH FOR
Watch for acceptance criteria that get edited the same day the first output arrives.

How do you set up a reviewer that starts cold?

Separate reviewer. Limited view.

The reviewer is a different agent, a different session, or a person. It gets the output, the criteria, and the evidence to judge them, such as the prospect’s current LinkedIn profile.

It never gets the conversation that produced the work. That limit is the point. A reviewer that never saw the reasoning can only agree with the evidence.

// WATCH FOR
Watch for a "separate" reviewer that is handed the full drafting thread as context.

What should the reviewer check that tests miss?

The rules that hold for every task.

Tests check what they were written to check. The failures that hurt usually sit outside them. Give the reviewer a short standing list that applies to every output, whatever the task.

  • No internal note, credential or pricing detail in anything a prospect can see
  • No prospect or client named in a public asset
  • No message to an account with an open deal
  • No claim about the prospect that the evidence does not support
// WATCH FOR
Watch for a workflow where every test passes and nobody has checked one of these.

What happens when the reviewer finds something?

A finding blocks the output and cites its evidence.

The output does not ship. The finding goes back with the specific message, the rule it broke, and what the reviewer saw. The work gets fixed and checked again.

Two habits keep this honest. A finding without evidence is dropped. A finding with evidence gets fixed, never explained away. If the rule itself was wrong, change it in writing and rerun the review.

// WATCH FOR
Watch for findings closed with a comment and no fix.

What should you ask a vendor about how they review AI work?

Three questions separate a review process from reassurance.

  1. Who checks the work, and did they build it?
  2. What do they check it against, and when was that written?
  3. What does the check look for that the tests do not?

A real answer names a separate reviewer, a written standard that predates the work, and a list of standing rules. "Our team reviews everything" names none of them.

Magnetiz builds this way. The review step never reviews work it produced, and the criteria are written when the task is created.

The pattern across independent review

Each step removes one way for the work to grade itself. The standard is fixed before the work starts. The reviewer never sees how it was made. The standing rules cover what the tests forgot. Findings carry evidence and block until fixed.

None of it requires reading code. It requires deciding, in writing, what good looks like before the AI does anything.

The work you didn’t watch is only as safe as the reviewer that didn’t build it.

Frequently asked questions

How do you review AI agent output?

Write acceptance criteria before the work starts, then give the output to a separate reviewer with only the criteria and the evidence. Add a standing list of rules every output must follow. Findings block the output until it is fixed.

Why shouldn’t an AI review its own work?

An AI reviewing its own work starts with the assumptions that produced it, so it tends to miss the same mistakes. A NeurIPS 2024 study found AI judges recognize and favor their own output.

What are acceptance criteria for AI agents?

Acceptance criteria for AI agents are the written conditions a passing output must meet, set when the task is created. Written first, they cannot bend to fit the output.

Do automated tests catch AI agent mistakes?

Automated tests catch the mistakes they were written to catch. Failures like a credential in a shared file or a message to an account in an open deal often sit outside them. A reviewer with standing rules covers that gap.

What should you ask an AI vendor about quality control?

Ask who checks the work and whether they built it, what they check it against and when that was written, and what the check looks for beyond the tests.
